name: sha256sum
one_line: compute and check SHA256 message digests
plain: `sha256sum` gives a file a 64-character fingerprint. It works like md5sum but uses SHA-256, which is still considered strong, so it is the right check for downloads, forensic evidence and software releases.
A published SHA-256 lets you prove a file is exactly what its author released.
when: Verify a downloaded ISO or tool.
Record the fingerprint of evidence in a forensics task.
Hash a string for a challenge.

examples.title: Hash a file
examples.explain: 64 hex characters then the name. Compare it with the value on the download page.

examples.title: Hash text
examples.explain: printf avoids the trailing newline that echo adds.

examples.title: Verify with a checksum file
examples.explain: Prints OK or FAILED per file.

examples.title: Verify only the one file you downloaded
examples.explain: Official checksum lists mention many files; this skips the ones you do not have.

examples.title: Compare to a known value
examples.explain: The two spaces between hash and name matter. Prints kali.iso: OK when equal.

examples.title: Hash everything below a folder
examples.explain: One file per line, ready to verify later with -c.

options.plain: Verify hashes listed in a file.
With -c, no output; exit code only.

mistakes: Using one space instead of two in a hand-written checksum line.
echo vs printf: echo adds a newline and changes the hash.
Copying a hash from a web page with an extra space or line break.
Assuming a matching hash proves safety: it proves sameness with whatever hash you compared to.
try: Hash a file, change one byte, hash again.
Verify a downloaded file against a checksum page.
Write a checksum list for a folder and verify it.
see_also: md5sum(1), sha1sum(1), sha512sum(1), b2sum(1), openssl(1), gpg(1) for signatures.
captured_with: Examples are written to explain a technique; they are not captured output.
